reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the CNS
clinicalPearls: The commonest malignant embryonal brain tumour of childhood, typically arising in the cerebellum and presenting with signs of raised intracranial pressure and truncal ataxia
Now classified into four molecular groups: WNT-activated, SHH-activated, and the provisional non-WNT/non-SHH group 3 and group 4, each with distinct biology and outcome
WNT-activated tumours carry the most favourable prognosis, whereas group 3 (often MYC-amplified) tends to behave most aggressively
Leptomeningeal (CSF) dissemination is common, so craniospinal MRI and CSF cytology are essential for accurate staging before treatment
Histological patterns include classic, desmoplastic/nodular, extensive nodularity, and large-cell/anaplastic forms, the last carrying a worse outlook
Desmoplastic/nodular and extensive-nodularity morphology is enriched in the SHH group, including infants and germline predisposition syndromes
Standard management combines maximal safe surgical resection, craniospinal radiotherapy (age-permitting), and multi-agent chemotherapy, stratified by risk
reference.pathophysiology: Medulloblastoma is an embryonal tumour thought to arise from progenitor cells of the cerebellar and brainstem region, including granule-cell precursors of the external granular layer and cells of the rhombic lip. Distinct molecular groups reflect dysregulation of key developmental signalling pathways: constitutive WNT signalling, aberrant sonic-hedgehog (SHH) pathway activation, and the less well-defined group 3 and group 4 tumours characterised by transcriptional and epigenetic changes with frequent MYC or MYCN amplification. Germline predisposition may underlie some cases, such as APC mutation in WNT tumours and PTCH1, SUFU or TP53 alterations in SHH tumours. The tumour has a strong tendency to seed the cerebrospinal fluid pathways, producing leptomeningeal metastases along the neuraxis.
additionalDifferentials: Metastatic small round blue cell tumour
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain to characterise the posterior fossa mass
Craniospinal MRI to assess for leptomeningeal spread before surgery where feasible
Lumbar CSF cytology (timed appropriately after surgery) for staging
Histopathology with molecular subgrouping (WNT, SHH, group 3, group 4)
Assessment for MYC/MYCN amplification and TP53 status
Germline testing for predisposition syndromes when clinically suggested
redFlags: Rapidly progressive raised intracranial pressure with obstructive hydrocephalus requiring urgent decompression
Reduced conscious level or signs of impending tonsillar herniation
Radiological or cytological evidence of leptomeningeal dissemination
Large-cell/anaplastic histology or MYC amplification indicating high-risk disease
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on molecular group, extent of resection, metastatic stage, and age. WNT-activated disease has an excellent prognosis, standard-risk non-WNT/non-SHH disease does moderately well with combined treatment, while metastatic, MYC-amplified group 3 and anaplastic tumours carry a poorer outlook. Long-term survivors frequently experience treatment-related neurocognitive, endocrine and growth sequelae.
pitfalls: Treating all medulloblastomas uniformly without molecular subgrouping, which now guides risk stratification and therapy de-escalation
Omitting craniospinal imaging and CSF cytology, leading to understaging of metastatic disease
Performing lumbar puncture before imaging in the presence of a posterior fossa mass and hydrocephalus
Underestimating the long-term cognitive and endocrine harm of craniospinal radiotherapy in young children
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
